title: Anger at home
hook: the gentle housewife Vedehika, her maid Kali, and the simile of the saw (MN 21)
tomorrow: someone used your good pen. why does it still sting an hour later?

segments.voice: Yesterday, strangers: the neutral person on the bus, filed away as scenery. They have a whole life. Today we come home, where the people are anything but neutral.

Patient with coworkers, polite to strangers, lovely online, and then someone at home asks the same question for the third time and it comes out sharp. The Buddha told a story about exactly this. In Savatthi lived a housewife named Vedehika, famous for being gentle. Her maid, Kali, a capable worker, wondered: is she really calm, or is it just that I do everything right? So Kali got up late. Vedehika frowned. Next day, later still. Vedehika spoke angrily. On the third day, later again, and Vedehika grabbed the pin from the door bolt and struck her on the head. Kali ran out into the street, bleeding, and told the neighbors.
screen: `SHARP, ONLY AT HOME.` → `A HOUSEWIFE FAMOUS FOR GENTLENESS.` → `KALI GETS UP LATE.` → `THE GENTLE ONE SNAPS.`

segments.voice: The gentle one snapped. And the Buddha's point is uncomfortable: someone is gentle only until unpleasant words reach them. Calm that's never been tested isn't calm yet. Home is where it gets tested, because home is where people get up late. So he offers a way to hear hard words. Speech can come at the right time or the wrong time, true or untrue, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, from goodwill or from hate. Five pairs. Anyone talking to you will land somewhere on them, and you can't control that. What you can train is your own mind in the gap before you answer. Then comes the simile this sutta is known for. Even if bandits were cutting someone limb from limb with a two-handled saw, the Buddha says, whoever let hate fill their mind would not be following his teaching. It's an extreme picture on purpose. If the saw doesn't justify hate, the dishes in the sink, the question asked three times, and the late start don't either. That doesn't mean swallowing everything. It means one thing first, before the sharp word: pause.
screen: `GENTLE UNTIL TESTED.` · `FIVE WAYS WORDS CAN COME.` · `THE TWO-HANDLED SAW.` · `IF NOT FOR THAT, NOT FOR THIS.` · then, large: `PAUSE.`

segments.voice: Sit as if you're at your own kitchen table, both hands flat on your thighs or a table. Bring back the last sharp word you said at home, or nearly said. Replay the moment just before it, and this time stop there: hands flat, one slow breath out, and let the word stay unsaid.
Anger at home: where gentleness gets tested, like Vedehika's, and where the pause matters most.
Keep this close: pause, one breath, before the sharp word. One of nine on the mind at home.

screen: `DAY 1608 COUNTS.` → `THE MIND AT HOME · 1 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES THE PEN STILL STING?`

howItsDone: Buddhists practice restraint of speech as part of right speech; teachers sometimes use MN 21's five ways of speaking and the simile of the saw to train patience, khanti, at home and in community.

match.prompt: the kitchen and the saw — tap the pairs.
pairs: the maid who got up late to test her
timely, true, gentle, helpful, kind, or not

myth: in the story, Vedehika stays calm when Kali tests her
she frowns, then speaks angrily, then strikes Kali with the door-bolt pin.
the Buddha says someone is gentle only until unpleasant words reach them
calm that has never been tested isn't proven yet.
the simile of the saw means taking any harm without protest
its point is the mind: not letting hate fill it, even then.

fork.setup: your roommate leaves the same mess for the third night. you're tired, and the sharp text is already typed. what does MN 21 suggest?
options: send it; it's true, and true words are always right speech.
delete it, say nothing ever, and quietly clean it yourself forever.
pause, wait for a calmer moment, then say it kindly and plainly.
fork.reveal: true isn't enough: the five pairs also ask about timing, gentleness, helpfulness and goodwill. pausing isn't silence forever.

original.note: Pali: patience, forbearance; the quality MN 21 trains.

trapdoor: what you thought: anger at home is normal, so it doesn't count.
what it means: home is where gentleness gets tested; the practice is to pause before the sharp word.
what a scholar hears: MN 21, the Kakacupama Sutta, sets the Vedehika story beside five pairs of speech and the simile of the saw.
guess: where gentleness gets tested, and the pause matters most
a sign that a family is broken beyond repair
fine to show, since family has to forgive you

chat.says: mom asked about college forms 3 times while i was cutting a mat. i snapped. she went quiet. now what?
options: Go say sorry. Next time she asks, pause first, and ask if later's a better time.
Nothing. She kept pushing, so snapping was fair and it doesn't count.
Promise never to feel angry again; real Buddhists don't feel anger at all.
chat.meaning: Vedehika shows gentleness gets tested at home. MN 21 trains the pause, and right timing is one of its five ways of speaking.

tie.story: Vedehika seemed gentle until Kali tested her, and the Buddha said calm is proven only when tested.
tie.friend: Mai can apologize to her mom, and next time pause and ask for a better moment.
tie.you: where at home does your gentleness get tested most?

Savatthi.meaning: a city where the Buddha stayed and taught

Vedehika.meaning: a housewife famous for gentleness, in a story the Buddha told

Kali.meaning: Vedehika's maid, who tested her calm

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta: the housewife Vedehika and her maid Kali; five courses of speech; the simile of the saw)

notes: MN 21 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the Vedehika story beats (three days, frown, angry words, the door-bolt pin, Kali bleeding and telling the neighbors) and that it's set in Savatthi.
The story includes a servant being struck; it is told plainly and briefly, with no detail beyond the sutta's.
'Calm that's never been tested isn't calm yet' and 'If the saw doesn't justify hate, the dishes don't either' are interpretive lines drawn from the sutta's argument; confirm.
Practice (body posture): hands flat, replaying a sharp moment and pausing; confirm it is gentle enough for people with hard home situations.
